[Konstantin Kakaes](https://www.quantamagazine.org/authors/konstantin-kakaes/), writing in [Quanta Magazine](https://www.quantamagazine.org/why-the-legendary-erdos-problems-are-falling-to-ai-20260803/), traces how the problems of Paul Erdős became the proving ground for AI mathematics, and what that has done to the community that formed around them.

What the article reports:

- **[Erdős](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Erdos/) and his prizes.** He posed thousands of problems in papers and letters to mathematicians around the world, often attaching cash prizes he paid out of pocket. The reward might be a token \$10 or \$25, or, for problems he considered important or difficult, it could range into the thousands. He traveled constantly and owned almost nothing, wore only silk, avoided being touched, called God the "Supreme Fascist," and fueled his output with amphetamines. He died of a heart attack in 1996 at a conference in Warsaw, and an Iowa nonprofit [has promised](https://www.combinatoricsfoundation.org/erd%C5%91s-problems) to keep paying his bounties. His prizes are now discussed in terms of per-problem token cost.

- **The list started as a personal project.** [Thomas Bloom](http://thomasbloom.org/), an arithmetic combinatorialist now at the University of Manchester, began collecting Erdős problems in early 2023 so he could keep track of which were still open. He used ChatGPT to write the Python behind [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/) and launched it with a couple hundred problems, "kind of with the expectation that maybe nobody would use it." Much of his work was editorial: Erdős often stated problems ambiguously, and Bloom decided what the most sensible version of each should be. *Over 2024 and the first eight months of 2025, 111 problems moved from open to solved*, though for several the change reflected a proof rediscovered or verified rather than newly found. At publication the database held 565 solved problems and 652 open ones.

- **A comment section turned it into a community.** Bloom added commenting in August 2025, again with ChatGPT-written code, by which point he had cataloged nearly 1,000 problems. Much of the activity came from outside academia. [Wouter van Doorn](https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/user/Woett?all_posts=1), the fourth-most-prolific commenter, works at a customer-service company and came close to finishing a master's in math at KU Leuven a decade ago. He took a six-month leave in 2024 to focus on math, reasoning that "Right now I'm still better at mathematics than an AI is, but who knows what it'll be in a year, two years, five years?" In October 2025 he left the first comment on [Problem 1102](https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/1102?order=oldest), which Erdős posed in 1981 about sets of square-free integers, and in early November posted progress he had worked out without AI. The commenter who claimed to find a flaw in it, and then conceded the argument, was [Terence Tao](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~tao/).

- **Hobbyists produced the first AI resolutions.** Kevin Barreto, a University of Cambridge undergraduate, and Liam Price, who studied some math in college but left before finishing, met in the summer of 2025 on a Discord server devoted to AI. In December 2025 they started feeding batches of problems to GPT-5.2. The model made little headway when told a problem was unsolved, so they learned to "prompt it in a very particular way, gaslighting it into thinking the problem is easier than it actually is."
    - Their first claim went up on Christmas morning on [Problem 333](https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/333?order=oldest), billed as "the first case of an LLM fully autonomously resolving an Erdős problem." The claim collapsed within hours when another user found that Erdős himself had [resolved it in a 1977 paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0022314X77900038). Barreto asked the site's members "to put greater focus on literature search on the problems currently marked as open," and added: "As someone who has fallen for this twice now, it's quite gut-wrenching."
    - [Problem 728](https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/728?order=oldest) held. On January 4, 2026 they used GPT-5.2 Pro to solve it, certified the proof in [Lean](https://lean-lang.org/) using [Harmonic](https://harmonic.fun/)'s Aristotle, and [Nat Sothanaphan](https://arxiv.org/a/sothanaphan_n_1), the site's most prolific participant, [wrote up the formalized result](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07421).
    - Price's method was to ask a chatbot for a solution, paste it into a fresh instance to check the previous one's work, and repeat until it held. The article notes this is the loop that labs automate as a harness or scaffold.
    - By his own assessment Price does not have the mathematics to verify the solutions he coaxes out of the models, so Barreto's contacts supply mathematicians who can.
    - Bloom was surprised that most of the new results had come from hobbyists and undergraduates using publicly available large language models (LLMs) rather than from the labs, which were paying attention and had better internal models.
    - Both are now co-authors with Tao, [Jared Duker Lichtman](https://mathematics.stanford.edu/people/jared-duker-lichtman) of Stanford, and other established mathematicians on a paper [resolving Problem 1196](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.00301), about the possible size of primitive sets.

- **Then the labs arrived.**
    - In January a [Google DeepMind](https://deepmind.google/)-led team of 24 published a Gemini case study that [screened 700 problems marked "Open"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.22401). The study addressed 13 of them, five through apparently novel solutions and eight by identifying solutions already in the literature. The paper's conclusion is that its findings "suggest that *the 'Open' status of the problems was through obscurity rather than difficulty*."
    - In May a separate 21-person DeepMind team reported that its agent [autonomously resolved 9 of 353 open problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22763) at a few hundred dollars each, searching only among problems already written in formal logic.
    - On May 20 [OpenAI](https://openai.com/) published a [counterexample to Erdős's 1946 unit distance conjecture](https://openai.com/index/model-disproves-discrete-geometry-conjecture/), found by an unreleased internal model, alongside [companion remarks](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/74c24085-19b0-4534-9c90-465b8e29ad73/unit-distance-remarks.pdf) from nine mathematicians. [Tim Gowers](https://www.college-de-france.fr/en/chair/timothy-gowers-combinatorics-statutory-chair/biography) wrote that "if a human had written the paper and submitted it to the *Annals of Mathematics* and I had been asked for a quick opinion, I would have recommended acceptance without any hesitation. No previous AI-generated proof has come close to that." The author line read simply "OpenAI." Human mathematicians substantially improved on the result within weeks.
    - Techniques related to that proof then let four mathematicians including Bloom [disprove the sum-product conjecture for real numbers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28781), a [long-suspected constraint linking addition and multiplication](https://www.quantamagazine.org/the-sum-product-problem-shows-how-addition-and-multiplication-constrain-each-other-20190206/). The integer case remains open.
    - On August 1 OpenAI [announced](https://openai.com/index/ten-advances-in-mathematics/) that an unreleased model named Astra had made ten further advances, three of them Erdős problems.

- **Why these problems.** Erdős's problems are mostly in number theory, combinatorics, and graph theory, the areas that have proved most tractable for LLMs. They also range widely in difficulty and significance, which suits a technology whose abilities range just as widely. Lichtman is direct about what the labs saw in Bloom's site: "This kind of single repository that anyone can access — labs realized that this could effectively be a benchmark."

- **The costs are already visible.** Bloom describes a flood of AI-written papers running 100 to 200 pages: "no human has read it, and no human is going to read it. It's a huge challenge now." [Noga Alon](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~nalon/) of Princeton, who has solved dozens of Erdős problems, has stopped trying: "Once AI started to solve them, there is no point anymore." Tao has stepped away from the site to focus on getting his own work done. In July 2026, on the day he was [awarded the Fields Medal](https://www.quantamagazine.org/jacob-tsimerman-wins-2026-fields-medal-for-andre-oort-conjecture-proof-20260723/), [Jacob Tsimerman](https://www.math.utoronto.ca/~jacobt/) announced he was leaving academia for OpenAI. Van Doorn says the models are "clearly better at thinking and doing math than I am." He is still at it anyway: "*If you want to play piano, you aren't going to hire a piano-playing machine that does it better than you.*"

One episode the article leaves out: in October 2025 an OpenAI researcher publicized GPT-5 finding solutions to open Erdős problems, and the solutions turned out to be published work the model had located. By [Gary Marcus's account](https://garymarcus.substack.com/p/erdosgate), which named the episode *Erdősgate*, [Demis Hassabis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demis_Hassabis) called the claim embarrassing and the post came down.

## My Notes

- **Some solved problems were only looked up**: on Bloom's site "open" means nobody has found a published solution. The label reports the state of the literature, so retrieving the prior paper flips it without any new mathematics. Erdősgate happened because nobody separated a new proof from a found citation. Both recent papers do. The [January study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.22401) counted novel proofs apart from the solutions it located in the literature, and [OpenAI's August paper](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/ten-proofs-oai.pdf) credits in its abstract the prior results each proof builds on. Counts can still move: one January solution first called novel was reclassified as a rediscovery two arXiv revisions later. Anyone reporting Erdős totals should say how many came out of a literature search.

- **The unit distance proof meets Gowers's criterion for depth**: in [The Two Cultures of Mathematics](https://www.dpmms.cam.ac.uk/~wtg10/2cultures.pdf) Gowers rebuts the charge that combinatorics is a shallow subject. A good problem stands in for a recurring difficulty, so its value goes "beyond merely finding out whether the answer to it is yes or no." General principles also transfer between combinatorial proofs where no formal dependence exists. A machine proof can be put to that test. A week after OpenAI's counterexample appeared, four mathematicians used related techniques to disprove the sum-product conjecture for real numbers.

- **Bloom's curation made the list gradable**: a model cannot be scored on a question nobody has stated precisely, or on a corpus with no status field. Supplying both was editorial work rather than mathematics. Someone had to resolve Erdős's prose into one defensible reading per problem, and that step comes before the Lean formalization that usually gets the credit. Most of mathematics has had neither step done. The labs have started paying for both. [Formal Conjectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.13171), from a DeepMind-affiliated group, is 2,615 Lean 4 statements, 1,029 of them open, built around what its authors call "a structured interface connecting mathematicians who formalize and clarify problems with the AI systems and humans attempting to solve them." Outside mathematics the same shortage is already a business: [Pramaana Labs](/posts/20260621-pramaana-formal-verification/) raised \$27M to formalize tax and statute into Lean, where the interpretive choices are both the product and the main risk.

- **Fewer mathematicians are willing to check**: Price cannot check his own output, so Barreto's contacts pass it to mathematicians who can, Tao among them. Tao has since stepped back from the site, and Alon, who has solved dozens of these problems, has stopped working them. [Tao's decomposition](/posts/20260422-proof-generation-vs-digestion/) treats digestion as the slow step, and assumes someone is still there to do it. Bloom's unread 200-page papers show what happens when nobody is.
